content: 1. The confidence intervals in some studies were imprecise, which may limit the reliability of the findings. This could be due to small sample sizes or a limited number of events observed in the studies. 2. Studies with a high risk of bias contributed to findings where less than 50% of the data was derived from reliable sources, further reducing the certainty of the results. 3. In the comparison of delayed pushing versus immediate pushing in women receiving epidural analgesia, the evidence from Lemos et al. (2017) suggested a moderate certainty of effect, with a reduction of 7 fewer events per 1,000 participants (ranging from 17 more to 27 fewer). However, the findings were deemed critical for clinical decision-making. 4. Severe, unexplained heterogeneity was observed in some studies, which could not be accounted for, further complicating the interpretation of the results. 5. Perineal massage during the second stage of labor, compared to usual care or a hands-off approach, was associated with 112 fewer events of perineal trauma per 1,000 participants (ranging from 7 more to 177 fewer). However, the certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to wide confidence intervals and high risk of bias in the included studies. 6. The use of warm perineal compresses compared to usual care or a hands-off approach showed a moderate certainty of evidence, with 9 fewer events per 1,000 participants (ranging from 14 more to 25 fewer). The findings were considered critical for clinical practice. 7. The hands-off approach to perineal management, compared to the hands-on approach, demonstrated a low certainty of evidence, with 61 fewer events of perineal trauma per 1,000 participants (ranging from 31 fewer to 83 fewer). The wide confidence intervals and unexplained heterogeneity reduced the reliability of these findings. 8. Ritgen’s maneuver, compared to usual practice (hands-on approach), was associated with 31 fewer events of perineal trauma per 1,000 participants (ranging from 5 more to 60 fewer). The certainty of evidence was low due to small sample sizes and wide confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect. 9. A selective or restrictive episiotomy policy, compared to routine or liberal use, showed low certainty of evidence. The findings indicated 18 more events per 1,000 participants (ranging from 21 fewer to 69 more) in one outcome and 14 fewer events per 1,000 participants (ranging from 4 more to 26 fewer) in another. The evidence was limited by small sample sizes and unexplained heterogeneity. 10. Manual fundal pressure during the second stage of labor, compared to no fundal pressure, was associated with 38 more events per 1,000 participants (ranging from 39 fewer to 162 more). The certainty of evidence was rated as very low due to wide confidence intervals, small sample sizes, and high risk of bias in the included studies. 11. In some cases, no events were observed, or the data could not be pooled due to methodological limitations, further reducing the reliability of the evidence.
